name: SUM

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range to add.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Adds all the numbers in a range of cells.
intro: SUM is the most-used function in Excel. It adds numbers in cells, ranges, or a mix of both — and it ignores text and empty cells, so you can select an entire column without cleaning it first.

examples.title: Sum a column
examples.note: A contiguous range is the fastest way to total a column.

examples.title: Sum individual cells
examples.note: Separate non-adjacent cells with commas.

commonErrors.cause: A referenced cell contains an error or text that can't be read as a number.
commonErrors.fix: Check the range for error values like #DIV/0! and fix those first.

name: COUNT

params.name: value1
params.description: The first item or range to count.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional items or ranges.

summary: Counts how many cells in a range contain numbers.
intro: COUNT tells you how many cells in a range hold numeric values. Text, blanks and logical values are skipped — use COUNTA instead if you need to count non-empty cells of any type.

examples.title: Count ignores text
examples.note: Only the numeric cell is counted.

name: COUNTA

params.name: value1
params.description: The first cell or range to count.

params.name: value2
params.description: Additional cells or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Counts how many cells in a range are not empty.
intro: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell — numbers, text, dates, errors and even formulas that return an empty string. It is the quickest way to check how much data a column actually holds, which makes it ideal for validating imports and form responses.

examples.title: Count filled cells
examples.note: The blank cell is skipped; text and numbers both count.

examples.title: Check a form column is complete
examples.note: Pair COUNTA with IF to flag incomplete lists.

commonErrors.cause: Cells containing spaces or formulas returning "" are not empty.
commonErrors.fix: Use TRIM to remove stray spaces, or COUNTBLANK to find visually-empty cells.

name: AVERAGE

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range to average.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges.

summary: Returns the average (arithmetic mean) of its arguments.
intro: AVERAGE adds up the numeric cells in a range and divides by how many there are. Like SUM, it ignores text and empty cells — but a 0 counts, so a blank and a zero give different results.

examples.title: Average with a blank cell
examples.note: The blank is skipped entirely — the divisor is 2, not 3.

commonErrors.cause: The range contains no numeric values.
commonErrors.fix: Make sure at least one cell in the range holds a number.

name: VLOOKUP

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to search for in the first column of the table.

params.name: table_array
params.description: The range of cells that contains the data.

params.name: col_index_num
params.description: The column number (counting from the left of table_array) to return.

params.name: range_lookup
params.description: TRUE for approximate match, FALSE for exact. Defaults to TRUE.

summary: Looks up a value in the first column of a table and returns a value in the same row from another column.
intro: VLOOKUP is Excel's classic lookup function: give it a key and a table, and it walks down the first column until it finds a match, then returns the value from whichever column number you specify. It is fast to write but has two famous limits — it can only look to the right, and a hard-coded column index breaks when you insert columns. For new workbooks, XLOOKUP or INDEX+MATCH are more flexible.

examples.title: Find a product price
examples.note: FALSE forces an exact match — always use it for IDs and SKUs.

examples.title: Approximate match on a grade table
examples.note: TRUE finds the largest value less than or equal to the lookup; the first column must be sorted ascending.

examples.title: Lookup across sheets
examples.note: Prefix the range with SheetName! to pull from another worksheet.

commonErrors.cause: The lookup value is not in the first column — often due to extra spaces or mismatched types (number vs text).
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the value in TRIM, or use IFERROR to catch the miss.

commonErrors.cause: col_index_num is bigger than the number of columns in table_array.
commonErrors.fix: Check that the index counts from the leftmost column of the lookup range, not of the sheet.

commonErrors.cause: range_lookup was left as TRUE so Excel returned an approximate match.
commonErrors.fix: Add FALSE as the fourth argument for exact matching.

name: XLOOKUP

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to search for.

params.name: lookup_array
params.description: The range or array to search.

params.name: return_array
params.description: The range or array to return a value from.

params.name: if_not_found
params.description: Text or value to return instead of #N/A when nothing matches.

params.name: match_mode
params.description: 0 = exact (default), -1 = exact or next smaller, 1 = exact or next larger, 2 = wildcard.

params.name: search_mode
params.description: 1 = first to last (default), -1 = last to first, 2/-2 = binary search.

summary: Searches a range and returns an item from a second range — the modern replacement for VLOOKUP.
intro: XLOOKUP fixes nearly every VLOOKUP limitation: it searches any column (not just the leftmost), returns from a separate range so inserting columns never breaks it, defaults to exact match, can search right-to-left, and has a built-in 'if not found' message. It requires Microsoft 365 or Excel 2021+.

examples.title: Look up to the left
examples.note: The return column sits left of the lookup column — impossible with VLOOKUP.

examples.title: Custom not-found message
examples.note: No IFERROR wrapper needed.

examples.title: Return a whole row
examples.note: A multi-column return_array spills results into neighbouring cells.

commonErrors.cause: No match and no if_not_found argument was supplied.
commonErrors.fix: Add a fourth argument like "Not found" to make misses readable.

commonErrors.cause: lookup_array and return_array have different sizes.
commonErrors.fix: Make both ranges the same length (e.g. A2:A10 and B2:B10).

commonErrors.cause: The workbook runs in Excel 2019 or earlier, which lacks XLOOKUP.
commonErrors.fix: Use INDEX+MATCH or VLOOKUP for older versions.

name: INDEX

params.name: array
params.description: The range of cells or array constant to pick from.

params.name: row_num
params.description: The row position within array to return.

params.name: column_num
params.description: The column position within array to return.

summary: Returns the value at a given row and column position inside a range.
intro: INDEX does one thing perfectly: it fetches the cell at position (row, column) of a range. On its own it is a simple coordinate picker; combined with MATCH — which finds the position of a value — it becomes the most flexible lookup pattern in Excel, able to look left, right, up or down.

examples.title: Two-dimensional lookup
examples.note: Row 2 of the range is 'South', column 2 is 'Feb'.

examples.title: INDEX + MATCH lookup
examples.note: MATCH finds the row; INDEX returns the price. No column-index to break.

commonErrors.cause: row_num or column_num points outside the array.
commonErrors.fix: Check that positions are relative to the array, not the worksheet.

name: MATCH

params.name: lookup_value
params.description: The value to locate.

params.name: lookup_array
params.description: The single row or column range to search.

params.name: match_type
params.description: 1 = largest value ≤ lookup (sorted asc), 0 = exact, -1 = smallest ≥ lookup (sorted desc).

summary: Finds the position of a value inside a row or column.
intro: MATCH returns a number — the relative position of your lookup value in a range — rather than the value itself. That position is exactly what INDEX needs, which is why INDEX+MATCH is the classic flexible lookup pair. Use match_type 0 for exact matches; 1 and -1 require sorted data.

examples.title: Find the position of a name
Approximate position in sorted prices
examples.note: match_type 1 returns the largest value that is ≤ 40.

commonErrors.cause: No exact match exists, or the list is not sorted for match_type 1/-1.
commonErrors.fix: For exact lookups keep match_type 0; for approximate, sort the lookup array correctly.

name: IF

params.name: logical_test
params.description: Any expression that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

params.name: value_if_true
params.description: What to return when the test is TRUE.

params.name: value_if_false
params.description: What to return when the test is FALSE (defaults to FALSE).

summary: Returns one value if a condition is true and another if it is false.
intro: IF is the decision-maker of Excel: test a condition, return A when it holds and B when it does not. Nest IFs for more than two outcomes — or reach for IFS, which reads like a flat list of conditions and is far easier to audit.

examples.title: Nested IF for three grades
examples.note: For many branches, IFS is cleaner.

commonErrors.cause: Text compared with = is not case-sensitive, and numbers stored as text fail numeric tests.
commonErrors.fix: Convert text numbers with VALUE or check LEN/TRIM issues first.

commonErrors.cause: The logical test references an error cell.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the test with IFERROR.

name: IFS

params.name: logical_test1
params.description: The first condition to evaluate.

params.name: value_if_true1
params.description: Result returned when the first condition is TRUE.

params.name: logical_testN
params.description: Additional test/result pairs, evaluated left to right.

summary: Evaluates multiple conditions and returns the value for the first TRUE one.
intro: IFS replaces deeply nested IF statements with a flat list of test/result pairs. Excel stops at the first TRUE condition, so order your tests from most to least specific. Available in Excel 2019 and Microsoft 365 — for a final catch-all, end with TRUE as the last test.

examples.title: Grade bands
examples.note: The trailing TRUE acts as 'else'.

commonErrors.cause: No condition evaluated to TRUE.
commonErrors.fix: Add a final TRUE,default-value pair as a fallback.

commonErrors.cause: IFS does not exist in Excel 2016 or earlier.
commonErrors.fix: Rewrite as nested IF.

name: SUMIF

params.name: range
params.description: The cells evaluated against criteria.

params.name: criteria
params.description: The condition, e.g. ">100", "apples" or a cell reference.

params.name: sum_range
params.description: The cells to actually add; defaults to range.

summary: Adds the cells that meet a single condition.
intro: SUMIF sums only the rows that satisfy one test — 'add up sales for the East region', 'total invoices over $500'. The criteria range and the sum range can be different columns, which makes it perfect for category totals. When you need two or more conditions, step up to SUMIFS.

examples.title: Sum values above a threshold
examples.note: When sum_range is omitted, range is summed.

commonErrors.cause: sum_range is a different size than range — Excel silently shifts it.
commonErrors.fix: Keep sum_range the same shape and starting row as range.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria type mismatch, e.g. comparing numbers stored as text.
commonErrors.fix: Normalize the column type (Text to Columns or VALUE).

name: SUMIFS

params.name: sum_range
params.description: The cells to add.

params.name: criteria_range1
params.description: The first range to test.

params.name: criteria1
params.description: The condition applied to criteria_range1.

params.name: criteria_range2 / criteria2
params.description: Extra range/condition pairs — all must be TRUE.

summary: Adds the cells that meet several conditions at once.
intro: SUMIFS extends SUMIF to as many criteria pairs as you need — 'total sales for East AND January', 'invoices over $500 AND unpaid'. Note the argument order differs from SUMIF: the range to sum comes first. Every criteria range must be the same size as sum_range.

examples.title: Amount in a date window
examples.note: Two criteria on the same range create a between filter.

commonErrors.cause: A criteria range does not match sum_range's dimensions.
commonErrors.fix: Every criteria_range must have the same number of rows/columns as sum_range.

name: COUNTIF

params.name: range
params.description: The cells to evaluate.

params.name: criteria
params.description: The condition, e.g. "yes", ">=10" or a cell reference.

summary: Counts the cells that meet a single condition.
intro: COUNTIF answers 'how many?' with one condition — how many orders say 'shipped', how many scores beat 80, how many times a name appears (the classic duplicate check). Criteria support wildcards (* and ?) and comparison operators, which makes it far more flexible than a plain COUNT.

examples.title: Duplicate flag
examples.note: TRUE means the name in A1 appears more than once.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria contain leading/trailing spaces or the column mixes text and numbers.
commonErrors.fix: TRIM the data or match the cell's stored type.

name: COUNTIFS

params.name: criteria_range1
params.description: The first range to test.

params.name: criteria1
params.description: The condition applied to criteria_range1.

params.name: criteria_range2 / criteria2
params.description: Additional range/condition pairs — all must be TRUE.

summary: Counts the rows that meet several conditions at once.
intro: COUNTIFS is the multi-test version of COUNTIF: every pair adds an AND filter, so 'count East rows in January that are over $100' is one formula. It is the fastest way to sanity-check a filtered export without leaving the grid.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria ranges have different sizes.
commonErrors.fix: Every criteria_range must span the same number of cells.

name: LEFT

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to slice.

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to take from the start; defaults to 1.

summary: Returns the first characters of a text string.
intro: LEFT grabs a fixed-length prefix — the first 3 characters of a product code, the area code of a phone number, the first word when paired with FIND. Text functions return text, so wrap LEFT in VALUE when you need the number back.

examples.title: First word of a name
examples.note: FIND locates the space; subtracting 1 drops it from the result.

commonErrors.cause: Hidden spaces or non-printing characters inflate the prefix.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap text in TRIM/CLEAN first.

name: RIGHT

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to slice.

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to take from the end; defaults to 1.

summary: Returns the last characters of a text string.
intro: RIGHT pulls a suffix — file extensions, last-4 digits of an ID, the postal code at the end of an address. Combined with LEN and FIND it extracts everything after a delimiter, which is the standard way to get the last word of a phrase in older Excel versions.

examples.title: Text after the hyphen
examples.note: LEN minus the delimiter position gives the suffix length.

commonErrors.cause: num_chars counts characters, not words.
commonErrors.fix: Use LEN(text)-FIND(...) to compute the right length.

name: MID

params.name: text
params.description: The text string to slice.

params.name: start_num
params.description: The position of the first character to return (1-based).

params.name: num_chars
params.description: How many characters to return.

summary: Returns characters from the middle of a text string.
intro: MID is the scalpel of the text functions: start anywhere, take any length. It shines when the piece you need sits between two markers — extract the domain after '@', the middle segment of a code, or characters at a computed position from FIND.

commonErrors.cause: start_num is beyond the string's length.
commonErrors.fix: Guard with IF(start_num<=LEN(text), ...) or check with LEN first.

name: LEN

params.name: text
params.description: The text string (or cell) to measure.

summary: Returns the number of characters in a text string.
intro: LEN counts every character — including trailing spaces you cannot see. That makes it the best debugging tool for 'the VLOOKUP should have matched but didn't': a LEN of 9 on an 8-character SKU means stray whitespace, and TRIM is the fix.

examples.title: Spot hidden spaces
examples.note: The difference reveals one trailing space.

commonErrors.cause: LEN counts spaces and non-breaking spaces.
commonErrors.fix: TRIM removes regular spaces; SUBSTITUTE with CHAR(160) handles non-breaking ones.

name: TRIM

params.name: text
params.description: The text to clean.

summary: Removes leading, trailing and repeated inner spaces from text.
intro: TRIM strips the invisible clutter that breaks lookups and comparisons: leading spaces, trailing spaces, and double spaces between words. Run it on imported data before any VLOOKUP or COUNTIF — mismatched whitespace is the #1 cause of 'value exists but lookup fails'.

examples.title: Fix a lookup
examples.note: After TRIM, the padded key matches.

commonErrors.cause: The cells contain non-breaking spaces (CHAR(160)), common in web pastes.
commonErrors.fix: Use TRIM(SUBSTITUTE(A1,CHAR(160)," ")).

name: CONCAT

params.name: text1
params.description: The first text item or range to join.

params.name: text2
params.description: Additional text items or ranges (up to 253).

summary: Joins text items and ranges into one string — no delimiter support.
intro: CONCAT is the modern successor to CONCATENATE: it accepts whole ranges as well as individual cells, so =CONCAT(A1:C1) joins a row without listing each cell. It inserts nothing between items — when you need commas, spaces or a 'skip blanks' switch, use TEXTJOIN instead.

commonErrors.cause: The workbook runs in Excel 2016 or earlier.
commonErrors.fix: Use CONCATENATE or the & operator.

commonErrors.cause: CONCAT adds no separator between items.
commonErrors.fix: Insert literal separators (", ") or switch to TEXTJOIN.

name: TEXTJOIN

params.name: delimiter
params.description: The separator placed between each item, e.g. ", ".

params.name: ignore_empty
params.description: TRUE skips empty cells; FALSE keeps them.

params.name: text1
params.description: The first text item or range.

params.name: text2
params.description: Additional items or ranges.

summary: Joins text with a chosen delimiter and can skip empty cells.
intro: TEXTJOIN is CONCAT with manners: a real delimiter and an ignore_empty flag that prevents stray commas when the list has gaps. It is the go-to for building CSV rows, combining address parts, or producing 'A, B, C' lists from a column — all without helper cells.

examples.title: Skip the blanks
examples.note: With FALSE you'd get a double comma.

commonErrors.cause: TEXTJOIN requires Excel 2019 or Microsoft 365.
commonErrors.fix: Fall back to CONCAT with manual delimiters.

commonErrors.cause: The joined result exceeds the 32,767 character cell limit.
commonErrors.fix: Join fewer items or split the output.

name: TODAY
summary: Returns the current date, refreshed every recalculation.
intro: TODAY() returns the system date — no arguments. Because it recalculates whenever the workbook opens or changes, it powers rolling reports like 'invoices due in the next 7 days' or 'days since signup'. For a frozen timestamp, use Ctrl+; instead.

examples.title: Days overdue
examples.result: Number of days between the due date and today
examples.note: Format the result as General, not Date.

examples.title: Flag items older than 30 days
examples.note: The serial date in A1 stands in for any past date.

commonErrors.error: Result shows a date, not a number
commonErrors.cause: Subtracting dates inherits date formatting.
commonErrors.fix: Set the cell format to General or Number.

name: NOW
summary: Returns the current date and time, refreshed on every recalculation.
intro: NOW() is TODAY() with the clock attached — date plus time as a serial number. Use it for timestamps on logs, 'last refreshed' stamps on dashboards, or elapsed-time calculations. Remember it is volatile: the value updates at every recalc, so paste-values if you need to freeze it.

examples.title: Current timestamp
examples.note: Displays like 11/9/2026 17:43 depending on formatting.

examples.title: Hours since an event
examples.note: Multiply the day-fraction difference by 24.

commonErrors.cause: The cell is formatted as a number.
commonErrors.fix: Format as 'm/d/yyyy h:mm'.

name: DATE

params.name: year
params.description: A four-digit year.

params.name: month
params.description: Month number; values >12 roll into the next year.

params.name: day
params.description: Day number; values >month length roll forward.

summary: Builds a valid date from separate year, month and day values.
intro: DATE assembles a serial date from parts — essential when a system exports year, month and day as separate columns, or when you compute dates like 'the last day of next month' (=DATE(y, m+2, 0)). Its rollover behaviour is a feature: month 13 becomes January of the following year.

examples.title: Last day of next month
examples.note: Day 0 rolls back to the last day of the previous month.

commonErrors.cause: Two-digit years map to 1900s (e.g. 26 → 1926).
commonErrors.fix: Always pass a four-digit year.

commonErrors.cause: An argument is text rather than a number.
commonErrors.fix: Convert with VALUE or check the source column type.

name: DATEDIF

params.name: start_date
params.description: The earlier date.

params.name: end_date
params.description: The later date.

params.name: unit
params.description: "Y" years, "M" months, "D" days, "MD"/"YM"/"YD" partial variants.

summary: Calculates the difference between two dates in years, months or days.
intro: DATEDIF is a hidden gem — it exists in every Excel version but never appears in the function list. Feed it two dates and a unit code to compute ages ('Y'), contract lengths ('M') or 'days between'. The 'MD' unit has known quirks; prefer 'D' for plain day counts.

commonErrors.cause: start_date is after end_date.
commonErrors.fix: Swap the arguments or wrap in IFERROR.

commonErrors.cause: "MD" unit can return negative or wrong values in some builds.
commonErrors.fix: Use "D" and divide, or compute year/month separately.

name: MAX

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Returns the largest numeric value in a set.
intro: MAX scans a range and hands back the biggest number — top sales figure, latest serial date, highest score. Text and blanks are ignored, so it is safe over messy columns. For 'the Nth largest', use LARGE; for conditional maxima, MAXIFS or MAX + IF in older versions.

examples.title: MAX over mixed data
examples.note: Text is skipped entirely.

commonErrors.cause: All values are text or the range is empty.
commonErrors.fix: Convert stored-as-text numbers first.

name: MIN

params.name: number1
params.description: The first number or range.

params.name: number2
params.description: Additional numbers or ranges (up to 255).

summary: Returns the smallest numeric value in a set.
intro: MIN finds the floor of your data — lowest price, earliest serial date, minimum score. It pairs naturally with MAX to bracket a dataset, and with SMALL when you need the 2nd, 3rd or Nth lowest instead of the absolute minimum.

commonErrors.cause: All values are text or the range is empty.
commonErrors.fix: Convert stored-as-text numbers first.

name: LARGE

params.name: array
params.description: The range of numbers to rank.

params.name: k
params.description: The rank to return — 1 is the largest.

summary: Returns the k-th largest value in a set.
intro: LARGE answers 'top N' questions: the 2nd-biggest sale, the 3rd-highest score, the top-5 total when wrapped in SUM. It is the backbone of leaderboard formulas, and it ignores text and blanks so you can point it at a raw data column.

examples.title: Sum of top 3
examples.note: An array constant sums the top three in one step.

commonErrors.cause: k is bigger than the number of numeric values in array.
commonErrors.fix: Check COUNT(range) first, or clamp k.

name: SMALL

params.name: array
params.description: The range of numbers to rank.

params.name: k
params.description: The rank to return — 1 is the smallest.

summary: Returns the k-th smallest value in a set.
intro: SMALL is LARGE mirrored: it returns the Nth lowest value — second-cheapest price, third-shortest time. It is a quiet powerhouse for outlier hunting and 'bottom 10%' checks without sorting the sheet.

examples.title: Median via SMALL
examples.note: For odd-sized sets, k=(n+1)/2 gives the middle value.

commonErrors.cause: k exceeds the count of numeric entries.
commonErrors.fix: Compare k against COUNT(range) before ranking.

name: ROUND

params.name: number
params.description: The value to round.

params.name: num_digits
params.description: Digits to keep: 2 = cents, 0 = whole, -2 = hundreds.

summary: Rounds a number to a specified number of digits.
intro: ROUND actually changes the stored value — unlike cell formatting, which only changes how it displays. That distinction matters in money math: display-rounded cells can still sum to a wrong-looking total, while ROUNDed values add up exactly. Negative num_digits round left of the decimal point.

commonErrors.cause: Cells were display-rounded instead of ROUND-ed.
commonErrors.fix: Apply ROUND inside the formula before summing.

name: IFERROR

params.name: value
params.description: The formula or expression to evaluate.

params.name: value_if_error
params.description: What to return if value produces any error.

summary: Catches any formula error and returns a friendly fallback instead.
intro: IFERROR swallows #N/A, #DIV/0!, #REF!, #VALUE! and friends in one wrapper — the standard way to keep lookup misses and divide-by-zeros from wrecking a dashboard. Use it deliberately though: hiding every error can mask real data problems, so prefer fixing the root cause when you can.

commonErrors.cause: The wrapped formula itself is broken — IFERROR hides the clue.
commonErrors.fix: Remove IFERROR temporarily to see the real error.

name: TEXT

params.name: value
params.description: The number, date or value to format.

params.name: format_text
params.description: An Excel format code in quotes, e.g. "#,##0.00" or "mmmm yyyy".

summary: Converts a value to text in a specific number format.
intro: TEXT turns numbers and dates into formatted strings for concatenation: 'Total: $1,250.00', 'Due March 2027'. Once TEXT runs, the result is text — you cannot sum it — so apply it at the very last step, when a number becomes a message.

commonErrors.cause: Excel applies the workbook's locale — codes like "aaaa" mean "yyyy" in some locales.
commonErrors.fix: Use English format codes and test in the target locale.

commonErrors.cause: The format string is missing quotes.
commonErrors.fix: Always quote the format: TEXT(A1,"0.00").
